Retake Library

Retake design system

Round three. One game in five printed worlds that switch every week. Every part has one meaning and is drawn in every state, in all five worlds. Tap the people and buttons in the phones: they work.

SkeletonWorldsColourTypeSpaceComponentsDay objectsMechanicsResults and tabsCoversReport over timeFirst takeScreen sizesInstallHindi and accessYour choicesMotion

One skeleton under all five worlds

  1. 1
    Top barBack, the day's plate as the bar's title, help. The cover alone has the day count and the language.
  2. 2
    The questionThe screen's heading, at 104 px on every step in all five worlds.
  3. 3
    Who said it, and the keyOne named voice for the lines on the cards. One key; its icons repeat on every number.
  4. 4
    3 to 5 peopleIdentical before the choice: newsprint panels in Lugdi, Edmondson tickets in Station, playing cards in Jadugar, scorecards in Cricket, TV name captions in Rukavat. Two of them have the same record in mirrored words.
  5. 5
    One main buttonPinned at 748 px. It waits with what is missing, then turns yellow and names what happens.

The painting stays whole behind Lugdi. Text sits on small plates that hug it, never a band across the screen.

The worlds

Five printed worlds over one skeleton. Each brings its own paintings, objects and palette; the pick yellow and the focus ring are shared.

Lugdi लुगदी

Each day is the next issue of a 1970s Hindi pulp novel.

हर दिन सत्तर के दशक के एक हिंदी लुगदी उपन्यास का अगला अंक है।

Station स्टेशन

Each day is printed on Indian Railways enamel boards, tickets and charts.

हर दिन भारतीय रेल के इनेमल बोर्ड, टिकट और चार्ट पर छपा है।

Jadugar जादूगर

Dekhiye, dekhiye! Each day is one night of a travelling jadoo show in a small town.

देखिए, देखिए! हर दिन किसी छोटे शहर में आए जादू के शो की एक रात है।

Cricket क्रिकेट

Each day is a match at the old stadium under floodlights, called by the commentator.

हर दिन फ़्लडलाइट में पुराने स्टेडियम का एक मैच है, कमेंटेटर की ज़ुबानी।

Rukavat रुकावट

Each day is an evening in front of the 1980s family TV, until the announcer says "Rukavat ke liye khed hai".

हर दिन अस्सी के दशक के घर के टीवी के सामने एक शाम है, जब तक उद्घोषक न कहे, "रुकावट के लिए खेद है"।

Ghat Ka Sauda

One night run up the ghat.

Level 3 of 6
Anatomy
Masthead strip, issue roundel, the painting full bleed, the title printed on it, a small plate for the line and level.

paper, ink, title, red; Sarpanch 900 45; Hind; radius 0 and full
States
play, continue, see your score, first visit, hard day, loading
Access
Title is the h1. Roundel is an image named "Issue 214". Painting hidden from screen readers.

Jadugar

Playing card (person card)

Anatomy
Gilt-edged linen card stock: one gilt hairline at the card's edge, bright where it faces the light, and a soft shadow under it. The numbers stand in the top-left corner as the card's index, rank over suit: each number over its icon, printed in ink; the portrait, set a little into the card, beside them; the name; the line in Body, its opening quote hung in the margin.
Tokens
card stock, ink, gilt; radius 8; Headline numerals; Body line
States
rest, hover, pressed, picked (yellow printed over the card, a 2 px ink frame, lifted a little further, a paper tick on the portrait), held, focus, committing, revisited
Access
One stop per card: name and numbers spoken, the line as its description. The numbers are hidden from the screen reader; the spoken name carries them.

Show ticket stub (day plate)

Chandni Mandal
Anatomy
Card stock that hugs the troupe's name, in Label ink. The stub end carries one crimson diamond pip and a row of perforations; the far end is punched through, the hole ringed in brass; a notch in each short edge. At 200% the stub fills the bar and the hole is left out, so the name stays on one line.
Tokens
card stock, ink, crimson pip, brass ring; radius 0; the notches and the hole by mask
States
one state; never tappable
Access
The plate is the bar's title text; the perforations, notches and punched hole are paint.

The show bill and the cloth (result)

Show 214Score

Score 86

Show 214Score

Score 86

Show 214Score

Score 86

Anatomy
A handbill on card stock, centred under the cot's spotlight: the show number printed in card white on the crimson head band, a hairline edge with one gilt rule 6 px inside it, on a soft shadow, then the score filled in on a ruled line. A painted crimson velvet cloth with a gold fringe covers it and slides off to the right inside the bill's edge; the same cloth is left bunched and tied back at the right edge.
Tokens
card stock, ink, crimson, gold; painted cloth plates; Score 36; radius 0
States
covered, half way, drawn back (also the still state: only the gathered cloth)
Access
The score is the result screen's h1 and is in the page from the start; the cloth is paint, hidden from screen readers. At most 1.2 s, a tap skips it, and reduced motion shows only the gathered cloth, with no movement.

Cards turned face down (checks)

Anatomy
Each spent check is a small gilt-edged card laid face down on the row, a margin of card stock round its crimson back with a gold lattice. The pool holds what is left; spent cards leave a gold outline.

Cover states, sheets and the dialog

The "?" sheet

The report over time

The report never says which way a player leans. Early numbers are pulled towards zero, so day one is never harsh. A change counts only when the lean stays below the first two weeks by more than its normal wobble, three Sundays running. The exact line comes from the research (RSE-164), not from design. It is a change in the game's picks, never a claim about the person.

The First take

The parts the First take adds, drawn from the First take itself (demo.py): the opening cutscene, notes on the cards in each world's paperwork with the progress marker, and the result that closes each chapter.

Notes on the cards, with progress

Rank, for the seats

The private reading, after chapter 5

Every screen size

One page, built once, that rearranges itself by the space it gets, and the painting fills the screen at every size. Phones and upright tablets use the portrait painting. Anything wider than tall uses a wide painting composed with its subject on the left, and the game sits in a column over the open right side, on a soft dark fade, never a blur. The cards turn on their side when there is room, and the tabs become a rail.

Installed as an app

Installing on a phone (shown once, after the third day)

App icon and home-screen name

Icon options (one icon for both worlds)

The icon cannot change weekly, so it carries both worlds. No Equal Lens logo: The Equal Lens stays a small credit in About.

A. The day's ticketdefaultB. The issue roundelC. Two worlds, one punch

The name under the icon

The game is called Retake. Six letters stay whole under the icon on every phone.

   Retake

The same name on the home screen, link previews, share cards and the store. In the stores the title is "Retake: a daily fairness puzzle".

Reminder notification (only if the player turns it on)

At most 8 words, names only the day's object. On iPhone, reminders work only once the app is installed.

RetakeTonight: one seat left at the Tatkal counter

Hindi, large text and small phones

Your choices

Each open question drawn both ways. The default stands until you choose. The first two would change a rule in the rulebook.

Where the day plate sits (a rule change)

The rulebook says the top bar holds only back and "?". Putting the plate in the bar keeps every step the same height and carries the world into the first view.

Small phones (a rule change)

Four people with their lines cannot fit 360 x 640 without scrolling. The rule asks for no scroll.

Who says the loaded lines

Each set gets one named local voice with a portrait. You can rename them.

The twin wording

The equal pair differs only by one loaded word. A later day swaps the words between them.

Text over the paintings

Text needs a plate or a tint to read over a painting.

Button lettering

Hindi has no capitals, and the display face is hard to read small.

The red print edge on the live button

The rulebook allows one red edge under the live button in Lugdi, like misaligned print. A design review says it looks like a trendy web button, not print.

The last line of the day

"Issue 214 is out" can sound like cricket and says nothing about tomorrow.

Which practice number players see

Today it was 7 on the result, 41 on Sunday and 150 on the Board.

Station board colour

Yellow now means only your pick. Real station boards are often yellow; both are drawn from the same enamel plate.

A third script on Station boards

Real boards carry the local script too. You chose to show only the language picked.

How open the game is about what it hides

The game never shows which way you lean, and never says which days test you.

Sunday's shape

Sunday shows the week, the lean, one look-again pair and a note.

Hindi words still to test

Draft words, to try with 5 Hindi-first players before fixing them.

Station plates: always a station

Every Station plate is a real station name; the day's theme lives in the question and the voice.

The magician's call

The world speaks as the magician, "Dekhiye, dekhiye!". The rules keep exclamations for a real win, so for now the call is only on the world card.

Scoreboard numerals in Khand

The world spec puts Khand on the cover title and the scoreboard numerals. The rule allows a display face on the cover title only.

The English line on the interruption card

The rules ban "sorry" on screen. The line is a quote from 1980s television, and the announcer said "khed hai": we regret.

Lettering on the chapter title card

The display face is kept for the cover title. The chapter card is a title card too, so it could carry it.

How many checks in an over

An over is six balls. The shared puzzle gives three checks, so a full over doubles them.

The face on the chapter title card

Rozha One is kept to the cover title. The chapter card is also a title card, so it could carry it too.

The button outside a puzzle

Play, Share and Start are the curtain itself: crimson velvet in one gilt edge. A card-white button would match the people cards instead.

The name of the Board in Rukavat

The world's places are the family sofa and the slots in the schedule. "Viewers' choice" says what a ranking is.

Motion

Timings

Press feedbackwithin 100 ms
Pick160 ms, cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)
Colour change160 ms
Committing260 ms, then the next step
Sheet in, out420 ms decelerate, 260 ms accelerate
Result reveal420 and 680 ms beats, done by 1100 ms; a tap skips it
The steps100, 160, 260, 420, 680, 1100 ms: each 1.618 times the last

Signature moves

Lugdi: the result reprints the cover, red ink, then black, then paper white. Station: figures arrive on split-flap tiles. Jadugar: the result pulls a crimson cloth off the show bill. Cricket: the third umpire's screen holds "Decision pending" for a beat, then the score drops onto the scoreboard plate by plate. Rukavat: the interruption card cuts in with its tone, then the picture comes back with the numbers. Under reduced motion all are instant.
